beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — opens directly on the Claude UI; the ask lands answered.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Hussain, and this video is about Snowflake Cortex — running A.I. inside your database. Forty thousand support tickets sit in a Snowflake table. SQL can count them. It cannot read them. So I asked Claude where to start.

props.command: I have 40,000 free-text support tickets in a Snowflake table. What is the smallest useful thing Snowflake Cortex can do with them — and what does it cost me in complexity?

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — the hesitant writer states the whole idea and corrects the reel's actual misconception (Cortex as a platform to integrate → a SQL function).
beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea. Cortex is not another platform to integrate. It is a SQL function you already know how to call — the model comes to the data, not the other way round.

it corrects to 'The model comes to the data'
'One query. No pipeline.' lands and holds

props.text:
Cortex is a platform.
You already call it.
Your data travels.
One query.

beats.role_note: The gap: structured columns are queryable, the body column is not.
beats.narration_text: Your warehouse is excellent at the structured columns — ticket I.D., timestamp, region. It is blind to the one that matters: the body. Counting rows is easy. Knowing which ones are angry about billing is not.

show.event: table header draws: ticket_id | created_at | region | body
structured columns tick, one by one — queryable
the body column fills with grey free-text blocks, no tick
COUNT(*) = 40,000 lands crisp above the table
'how many are angry about billing?' sits under it, unanswered

beats.role_note: Pipeline vs in-warehouse inference — the governance argument.
beats.narration_text: The usual answer is a pipeline: export the text, send it to a model A.P.I., load the answers back — a second system, a second copy of your data. Cortex inverts it: the model runs inside Snowflake, and your grants still apply.

show.event: top lane draws: warehouse → export → model API → load back; a copy detaches
the detached copy flags warn-red: 'second system, second copy'
top lane dims; the Snowflake boundary draws below as one closed box
the model slides INSIDE the boundary, terracotta
'RBAC + grants unchanged' settles on the boundary wall

props.sparkLine: The model comes to the data.

beats.narration_text: So the starter use case is small enough to finish: ticket triage. Watch how ordinary the query looks.

show.event: spark alone above the composer — no greeting, this is a micro-beat
the triage ask types in
send arms, 'writing the query…' runs

props.command: Write the SQL that triages these tickets: a category, a sentiment score, and a one-line summary — in one pass over the table.

beats.role_note: ASK→RESULT receipt. Real Cortex SQL — ACTUAL-CODE discipline.
beats.narration_text: That is the whole thing. Three Cortex functions in a select list. CLASSIFY_TEXT picks from a label set you define. SENTIMENT scores minus one to plus one. SUMMARIZE writes the one-liner. No infrastructure anywhere.

show.event: code card fades in, 'triage.sql' in the title bar
CLASSIFY_TEXT block reveals, the label set highlighted
SENTIMENT line reveals
SUMMARIZE line reveals
the WHERE clause reveals last and holds — setup for B07

props.title: triage.sql — three functions, one SELECT
props.code:
-- One pass over the table. No pipeline, no export.
SELECT
    ticket_id,
    SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.CLASSIFY_TEXT(
        body,
        ARRAY_CONSTRUCT('billing', 'bug', 'feature', 'other')
    ):label::STRING                  AS category,
    SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.SENTIMENT(body) AS sentiment,
    SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.SUMMARIZE(body) AS one_liner
FROM support_tickets
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE());

beats.role_note: The result: three new columns, same warehouse, same grants.
beats.narration_text: The output is just a table. Same warehouse, same grants, three new columns you can group by. Billing complaints, sorted by how angry they are. That is a dashboard query now.

the grid re-sorts so the angriest billing rows rise to the top
'GROUP BY category' chip settles under the grid

beats.role_note: Teardown beat — the three honest failure modes the demos skip.
beats.narration_text: Now where it bites. You are billed per token, so a select-star over the whole table is a real invoice — that WHERE clause was doing quiet work. The labels are not deterministic. And a guess is not accuracy until you measure it.

show.event: three empty cost-cards draw across the stage
card one fills: 'Billed per token' — a token meter climbs as rows scan
card two fills: 'Not deterministic' — one ticket lands in two buckets
card three fills: 'A guess, until measured' — an unmeasured column greys out
all three hold side by side for the verdict

items.head: Billed per token
items.body: SELECT * over the full table is an invoice, not a test. Filter first — that WHERE clause was the cost control.

items.head: Not deterministic
items.body: The same ticket can classify differently across runs. Pin the label set; re-running is not free re-checking.

items.head: A guess, until measured
items.body: Hand-label a sample and score the model against it. Without that number you have vibes in a column.

beats.role_note: Verdict artifact page — UI beat, legal under ILLUSTRATE LAW.
beats.narration_text: The verdict. Cortex earns it when the alternative is a pipeline you never wanted. Filter before you classify, and measure before you trust it.

show.event: artifact window card springs in
heading 'Cortex, for a starter' settles
the four verdict lines stagger in, numbered
the card holds full for the read

artifactLines: Worth it when the alternative is a pipeline you never wanted.
Filter before you classify — the WHERE clause is the cost control.
Measure before you trust — a label set is not accuracy.
Best on problems where a rough label beats no label at all.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt typed, read aloud verbatim, then discussed.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: “Here is the schema of one text-heavy table I own. Show me the single Cortex query that would produce the most decision-useful column — then tell me what it costs per million rows, and how to validate the labels.” Those last two clauses are the point — anyone hands you the query, nobody the invoice.
